entries.title: Teens worldwide aren't getting enough exercise -- especially girls
entries.summary: A new study looks at the recommended amount of daily exercise for adolescents — and how few are getting it.
entries.content:
Teens worldwide aren't getting enough exercise — especially girls

The World Health Organization recommends adolescents spend at least one hour a day exercising enough to basically break a sweat — a brisk walk or a more intense pick-up soccer game. Lot's of research suggests this level of activity is crucial for supporting growing bodies and minds.

But new global data suggests only a small minority of kids and teens get that much. In fact, one in four report not hitting 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise any day of the week, according to a new study in The Lancet Global Health. Girls, as well as adolescents from middle- and lower-income countries reported even lower levels of exercise.

"The findings are disappointing, because one of the major results is that the trend over the last 15 years is flat," says Fiona Bull, head of the physical activity unit at the World Health Organization, who co-authored the study. "These data are a call for us to relook at what we're doing. Business as usual will not change these trends."

Changing habits in those teen years could have a lifelong impact, says Solveig Cunningham, a global health researcher at Emory University. "As an adolescent, if your baseline is zero days of physical activity, that's going to be your baseline as you go into adulthood."

What 3 million teens revealed

So how do researchers know whether adolescents are — or aren't — working up a sweat? It's tricky. Researchers would love to be able to strap smartwatches to kids to get detailed data, but that would be costly. The next best strategy is to ask a basic question — how many days during the past week were you active for at least 60 minutes?

The report draws on data from surveys posting some version of this question to over 3 million adolescents from 140 countries over the past 15 years. Only about 14% of kids worldwide reported getting an hour a day of exercise. Globally, the average adolescent reported less than 3 such days a week, the study found.

Kids from low- and middle-income countries tended to be less active than their counterparts from wealthier Western countries, the study found. There's no one explanation for this pattern, but a few likely causes stand out.

"Physical activity is an issue of opportunity," says Andrea Ramirez Varela, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas Health Science Center in Houston. In many lower income countries, she says that the environment — where they live, go to school and play — often restricts opportunities to be active. The study didn't break down the urban and rural divide, but some research suggests rural adolescents in lower-income countries move more, she says, often out of necessity. In increasingly populated urban areas, activity is lower.

Many cities aren't designed to be walkable, says Varela. In Latin America, where she does most of her research, "many parents think it's unsafe to just let your kids walk alone to and from places," she says — much less go out and play independently. In some urban centers, air pollution can make being active outdoors unhealthy too.

Screens may play a role as well. After school, "kids and adolescents, when they arrive home, they start watching TV, they are in front of a screen," says Valera. "Because this digital world is so attractive, they are going to be sedentary the rest of the day."

Cultural barriers

The report also revealed a stubborn gender gap.

Girls were less active than boys in virtually all countries. Nearly 30% don't exercise at all during the week compared to 22% of boys. Only 11% of girls were active daily compared to 17% of boys. And girls' weekly average of active days was lower (2.4 vs 3).

"It's very worrying to see this gender difference so early," says Bull, noting that the difference often persists into adulthood.

Different norms around what's appropriate for girls often drive that divergence.

"In many places, when girls reach puberty, there are taboos to engaging in physical activity," says Cunningham. Take India, for example, where Cunningham has focused much of her research. "Mothers or grandmothers will say, 'Well, you know, we don't want girls spending a lot of time outside. Their skin might get darker. That might have negative implications for whether they can get married."

Cunningham notes that girls are active in other, often less intense ways. "In South Asia, as well the United States, a substantial proportion of girls' active time is doing chores," she says "If the guys are outside playing and the girls are inside sweeping, they're both active, but it's kind of not the same thing."

What would get them moving?

Improving these trends won't be easy, experts told NPR. Redesigning cities to be more walkable, for instance, takes many years and substantial investment. Many experts point to schools as a practical place to start. "To move the needle, we need to focus on the settings where kids and adolescents spend most of their time," says Valera.

In fact, data suggests that countries with higher levels of adolescent exercise tend to have more structured time for sport during or after the school day. Building up such programs in other countries might help close the gap, says Valera, especially if done in ways that make sport accessible and affordable.

Such efforts will require sustained attention from policymakers, Valera says, who face pressures from all sorts of competing interests. But she says it's worth it.

"Not solving the problem in this stage of life will perpetuate the problem in adulthood," she says, where the costs to society, in terms of poor physical and mental health, only become greater.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: What's next for Democrats after the midterms. And, a look at the outstanding races
entries.summary: Democrats have regained control of Congress. They have a long list of investigations into Trump planned. And, not all races have been called. Here's a look at how they could affect the Dems' majority.
entries.content:
Democrats' First 100 Hours, Outstanding Midterm Races, Trump Doubles Down On Policies

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Democrats won this week in districts and states that President Trump carried by double digits just two years ago. The party now has its largest Senate majority since the passing of the Affordable Care Act during Obama's early presidency. Senate results from Alaska and Mississippi are still pending. If those races favor Democrats, their majority could grow to 54, plus the two independents who caucus with them.

  • 🎧 A few tight House races remain uncalled, but the swing toward Democrats already rivals the post-Nixon Watergate backlash, NPR's Tamara Keith tells Up First. She highlights two notable race surprises that happened this week. One was in Nevada's 2nd District, which has been Republican since the 1980s. Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson claimed victory overnight. The other was in Alabama's 2nd District, where Shomari Figures overcame redistricting that favored Trump by 14 points. Figures won by more than seven points.
  • ➡️ Mike Johnson plans to step down as top House Republican in the new Congress after a tough defeat for his party, according to a source familiar with his plans who was not authorized to discuss them publicly.
  • ➡️ Voters in 39 states, Washington, D.C., and the Northern Mariana Islands decided on 146 ballot measures covering issues like taxes, transgender rights, traffic cameras and data centers. Here's a summary of the results.

For more than a year, Democrats urged voters to elect them to lower costs and eliminate corruption. Now, the party must act to fulfill its campaign promise. The new Congress is unlikely to see much major legislation signed into law, but Democrats plan to launch ambitious investigations in the House and Senate. Democratic Party leaders and political analysts shared their insights with Morning Edition on the midterm election results, discussed the impacts of mid-decade redistricting efforts and outlined the party's next steps.

  • 🎧 Most legislation still requires 60 votes to pass the Senate, and Trump has fluctuated between saying he will be Mr. Veto and expressing willingness to work with Democrats, NPR's Sam Gringlas says. Democrats are interested in restoring enhanced ACA health subsidies, reversing Medicaid cuts, asserting control over tariffs and pushing to end the war with Iran. Gringlas says this election has intensified pressure on Democrats. He points to a voter he met this summer, who said that if Democrats gained control, they would have to enact real changes, otherwise it wouldn't matter who they nominated for president in 2028.

Trump focused on his East Wing ballroom construction project during his first public appearance after the Republicans lost the House and Senate. When asked about the election, he said he wasn't to blame for his party's losses.

  • 🎧 Trump quickly pointed out that he wasn't actually on the ballot, NPR's Emily Feng says. But he did urge voters to imagine he was. Voters associated his signature policies, like tariffs and the war in Iran, with rising inflation and gas prices. After Vice President JD Vance posted on social media yesterday suggesting that the war in Iran contributed to GOP losses, Trump somewhat agreed. The president cited its impact on pump prices, but doubled down on the war, saying he would act the same way again if he had to. With a Democratic Congress, Trump will encounter greater legislative gridlock, and Democrats could wield stricter funding controls on issues like immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict in Iran, Feng says.
  • ➡️ A new Democratic majority could pressure Trump to end the war in Iran. But directly influencing fuel prices, which are tied to the complex international oil market, will be challenging.

Life advice

Have you ever found yourself drowning in a sea of your own mail or other documents? Well, it is time to tackle that paper chaos. Don't panic. Kacy Paide, a professional organizer with more than 20 years of experience, has shared tips with Life Kit to make the task less overwhelming.

  • ✉️ Focus on your closest pile and separate it into active and inactive ones. Active items require follow-up, like calls or bill payments, while inactive items do not.
  • ✉️ Clearly mark the due date on active documents with a bold, permanent marker on a sticky note.
  • ✉️ Save important documents like birth certificates, passports, product manuals, tax papers and medical records. Choose a method that suits your habits: alphabetize, color-code or simply label. For easy access, place vital documents in a brightly colored folder.
  • ✉️ You don't need to shred everything that has your name and address on it. The Federal Trade Commission advises destroying documents containing sensitive information, such as account numbers, birth dates, passwords, signatures and Social Security numbers, to protect against identity theft.
  • ✉️ Start small by dedicating just 25 minutes to decluttering. Remember, organizing is an ongoing process that needs regular maintenance and adjustments.

Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Picture show

In Ukraine's Kherson region, a brief ceasefire brought a momentary return to normalcy. Brokered by first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo last week, the truce allowed hundreds of residents to evacuate from a Russian-occupied town and provided a rare few days of peace in a frontline city. Russia and Ukraine agreed to the deal to help Oleshky, a town near Kherson that was occupied by Russian troops in 2022. The troops had mined the land around it, and food and medicine were rarely able to reach the people. This short pause in hostilities was a welcome relief, allowing families to fill the sidewalks, shoppers to hurry to stock up and cafe-goers to enjoy art-filled spaces. These photos capture a brief glimpse of everyday life for these people.

3 things to know before you go

  • At Connecticut's Old State House, the annual Election Cake Bake-Off has been celebrating the sweet civic tradition of election cake for more than 250 years. This dessert has evolved from what it once was: a tough fruitcake, often soaked in alcohol.
  • Chemical manufacturer 3M has reached a $7.35 billion settlement to resolve thousands of personal injury claims related to toxic chemicals found in firefighting foam. (via PRE News & Ideas)
  • A new study shows that loon populations are declining across the birds' southern breeding range, but Maine stands out with a slight increase in loon productivity, according to Birds Canada. (via Maine Public)

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction
entries.summary: A federal panel will meet to consider the arch for final approval on Thursday, and the government said it may begin construction later that same day. Critics hope a judge will intervene last-minute.
entries.content:
Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction

This could be a make-or-break week for President Trump's triumphal arch.

For months, the Trump administration has barreled toward his dream of building a 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C.: rubber-stamping and side-stepping various federal reviews, cutting out Congress and announcing imminent construction despite a lack of final approval and an ongoing legal battle.

In May, the entirely Trump-appointed Commission for Fine Arts approved the arch's design — still incomplete at the time. In September, a federal council packed with Trump allies abruptly terminated a historic preservation review that participants had already criticized as rushed.

It all comes to a head on Thursday, when the National Capital Planning Commission will meet to consider final approval for the controversial structure. The arch is the only item on the agenda; the meeting will be online-only and is expected to take five hours because of the high volume of public participation.

Nearly 120 concerned citizens have signed up to speak, an unusually high number for such meetings and a symbol of the widespread public opposition. Democratic lawmakers, veterans, historic preservationists and more than 100,000 people have spoken out against the arch in written comments, local protests and previous commission meetings.

Among their many concerns, critics say the structure would obstruct an important view, insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital.

The White House has repeatedly said the arch will "enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery" and be "one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world."

"It will be one of the great things we've ever done," Trump said from the Reflecting Pool on Monday, giving the arch — alongside several other D.C. construction projects — valuable airtime in his last in-person remarks before the midterm elections.

The planning commission is widely expected to greenlight the arch. It approved preliminary site and building plans over the summer, and its new Trump-appointed chair, Mark Paoletta, expressed his enthusiastic support for the arch in an op-ed published last month. The administration says that after a successful commission vote, all that's needed to break ground is sign-off from its own Department of the Interior.

In fact, the government notified a federal judge late last month that, pending those two approvals, "construction could commence as early as" Thursday.

It filed that notice as part of the ongoing lawsuit brought by Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian who argue the arch is unlawful without approval from Congress. The Trump administration has not sought that, instead citing Congress' century-old authorization of a pair of columns on that traffic circle that were ultimately never built.

The plaintiffs promptly asked District Judge Tanya Chutkan to issue a preliminary injunction before Thursday's meeting to block the administration from "taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction, of any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization" while the case plays out.

A group of advocacy, historic preservation and conservation organizations quickly signed on to a supporting brief. At a hearing last Friday, Chutkan heard from both sides and expressed skepticism about the government's sense of urgency and national security claims. Then, over the weekend, D.C. and Virginia jointly filed their own lawsuit, calling the arch "flagrantly illegal" for a whole host of reasons.

Chutkan has consolidated the two cases, with all eyes on her docket as Thursday's meeting ticks closer.

On Monday, the judge ordered the government to notify the court within one hour of any arch decision by the National Capital Planning Commission, National Park Service and Department of the Interior — and to provide notice within 30 minutes of "any activity related to or in preparation for the construction of an arch on Memorial Circle."

Chutkan's order suggests she may wait to issue a ruling on construction until after the planning commission meeting, which is scheduled to adjourn at 6 p.m. ET.

On Tuesday, the Trump administration asked Chutkan to clarify and to modify her order to require 24 hours' notice instead, explaining that even though its staff is "working diligently (including nights and weekends) on this matter, it takes time for decisions to be communicated through the various chains and then appropriately drafted into a notice suitable for filing with the Court."

The plaintiffs responded with their own filings, opposing that request. They compared the situation to that at D.C.'s East Potomac Park, where the government provided the judge in that case less than a full day's notice before cutting down 430 trees during a holiday weekend.

"Indeed, Defendants recently demonstrated just how much they can change the status quo in a matter of 24 hours," the lawyers wrote.

The judge later clarified her wording but kept the timeline the same.

Hours later, on Wednesday night, the government notified the court that Grunley Construction Company, a Maryland-based firm, "may be — but is not necessarily — arranging off-site preparations for construction mobilization in anticipation of permit approval."

How we got here — and what could happen next

The first registered speaker on the meeting agenda is plaintiff Michael Lemmon, the veteran and retired foreign service officer for whom the lawsuit is named. Lemmon has said he hopes to be buried in Arlington National Cemetery one day — but not if there's an arch.

"The thought of being interred in the shadow of what I believe to be a personal vanity project is profoundly disturbing to me," he wrote in a court filing in February, when the case was first filed.

The arch would stand 250 feet tall in Memorial Circle, a traffic circle on the bridge that links D.C.'s National Mall to Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. It would be more than twice the height of the nearby Lincoln Memorial and, by the National Park Service's own admission, disrupt the historical significance of dozens of nearby monuments.

Renderings submitted to the planning commission show a white concrete structure topped with three golden statues, including a winged woman holding a torch with an eternal flame.

That flame was one of the recommendations of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which said in September that the arch would not pose a hazard to airspace as long as it is continuously lit a certain way. Aviation safety experts told NPR that those unconventional lighting recommendations add a new layer of risk — like glare and fire hazards — to an already troubling proposal.

Just days after the FAA released its report, Trump announced on social media that the arch would actually serve as a military complex housing snipers and ammunition. Legal experts saw that abrupt rebrand as an attempt to cast the arch as a matter of national security, an argument that has so far helped the administration proceed with its controversial White House ballroom. 

The final renderings sent to the planning commission don't mention drones or snipers. But in a seven-page declaration submitted to the court last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called the arch a "generational national defense opportunity."

On Friday, Chutkan questioned how the government would square installing military equipment with accommodating what it has said could be up to 22,000 civilian visitors per day.

"The arch is somehow supposed to deter assassination attempts on the president?" she said, in response to the government attorney's answers. "It's going to be completed three years from now."

As the legal battle over the arch intensifies, one of the Trump administration's primary arguments is that the veterans don't have standing to sue. They point to the Supreme Court's ruling in the ballroom case, though Public Citizen — the group representing the veterans — says the two are very different.

It's in that context that the Democrat-led governments of D.C. and Virginia jumped into the fray with their own lawsuit this weekend. Their 55-page complaint details their grounds for suing as well as the "battery of irreplaceable injuries" they say their communities will suffer "as soon as construction begins — from disruptions of local traffic to environmental degradation to threats to security and emergency preparedness."

The jurisdictions argue that the arch is illegal without congressional authorization and violates federal environmental and historic preservation laws as well as D.C.'s restrictions on building heights.

They say an arch would "substantially disrupt daily life in the capital region," including by forcing local governments to divert resources away from other priorities. The lawsuit says an arch at that location would increase traffic and hinder emergency response along one of the main corridors between D.C. and Virginia, complicate the flight path of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and threaten local wildlife, all things that governments would have to spend time and resources addressing.

They also have concerns about the construction process itself — from 320-foot cranes disrupting already-complex airspace to excavation work sending sediment into the Potomac River.

"These harms cannot be remedied if construction of the Arch proceeds," the complaint reads, adding that "the unlawful construction of a project of this scale will be difficult to undo."

The Trump administration has said construction will take two to three years, with crews working 20 hours a day, year-round. It said in a court filing last week that the first six months will involve underground excavation and foundation work, arguing that there is no need for a judge to intervene at this stage because plaintiffs' concerns about the lost view would not be relevant.

But lawyers for D.C. and Virginia say the administration "would suffer no cognizable injury if required to wait before beginning construction of an illegal monument."

"Defendants cannot plausibly claim they have an urgent need to begin building the Arch 101 years after enactment of the statute that they (wrongly) claim authorized its construction and over one year after the President announced his intention to build it," they wrote.

Critics have accused Trump of trying to rush approval of the arch before this week's midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers filed a supporting brief in the suit, with several vowing they will not let the arch proceed if their party retakes control of Congress.

entries.title: The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election
entries.summary: Tuesday's dramatic midterm results have transformed the electoral map, ensuring the path to future power for Democrats and Republicans must run through the South and its diverse voting population.
entries.content:
The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Tuesday's dramatic midterm results have transformed the electoral map, ensuring the future path to power for Democrats and Republicans alike must run through the South.

Black voter turnout surged in states like Louisiana and Georgia, as Democrats flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Mississippi is too close to call.

Republican-led efforts to redraw House districts to gain more favorable districts in places like Alabama, North Carolina, Texas and Florida backfired, with Democrats poised to net several seats in the region.

Loading...

In several states, the margins at the top of the ticket were so large that the blue tsunami carried down ballot races along with it, flipping several state legislative chambers and statewide offices along the way.

Even in contests where Democrats ultimately did not prevail, the millions of dollars of investment from both sides and the wide-ranging repudiation of the Trump administration from every demographic group highlight the South's important role in control of Congress and the White House in future election cycles.

Redistricting

In the aftermath of a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that gutted part of the Voting Rights Act, Republican-led Southern states rushed to redraw House maps to create additional seats that would better withstand a midterm environment where voters punished the party in power.

They included changes in Tennessee that split Memphis into three districts (and where Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson is within a few thousand votes of winning), a redraw of several Alabama districts that sought to unseat Rep. Shomari Figures (who won by nearly 8 points in the new Trump +14 configuration) and a target of nine seats in Texas and Florida.

Loading...

As of Wednesday night, Republicans have won one of them, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Before Election Day, there were signs that the ruling, along with the war in Iran, rising costs, concerns about corruption with the Trump administration and other top issues would serve as a motivator for turnout among Black voters.

In primaries held after the ruling, Black voter participation soared. Ashley Kennedy Shelton with the Louisiana-based Power Coalition for Equity and Justice previously told NPR that the court decision was "personal" for Black voters.

"Everybody's spending more money on their electricity bills, their gas bills, their food bills," she said. "All of these different things are really personally impacting voters. And I think that for all the folks that used to say, 'I don't do politics!' I think they realize that politics is absolutely doing them, and they have to get involved."

In South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews flipped a U.S. Senate seat, the state saw record voting for a gubernatorial election year, driven in part by elevated Black turnout. It's a similar story in Louisiana, where Democrat Jamie Davis narrowly lost to Sen.-elect Julia Letlow by less than two percent in a state Trump won by more than 15 points in 2024.

Mississippi's Senate race is too close to call, with Democrat Scott Colom leading by less than 1200 votes against incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state with the highest share of Black voters in the country.

Loading...

State level

It's not just Congress where the South is the center of shifting power. Big Democratic victories — or swings away from Republicans — at the top of the ticket led to an avalanche of shifting offices at the state and local level.

Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's 18-point victory in Georgia helped propel former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms to victory in the governor's race, as Democrats swept every single statewide elected office, gained control of the state utility regulator and are set to win a majority in the state House.

In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper's 20-point victory was enough to potentially flip multiple congressional seats and win control of the state House.

Texas Democrats won a majority of seats in their state House, while Republican House supermajorities in Florida and South Carolina have ended, too. The down ballot gains extend into states that aren't as purple or blue, with dozens more pickups reported in Alabama, Arkansas, Kentucky and Tennessee.

2028 is now

The expansive majorities in the House and Senate built upon southern swings have implications far beyond the makeup of the next Congress, as both parties look ahead to the 2028 presidential election.

In the leadup to Election Day this year, potential presidential contenders from both parties have made varying efforts to offer financial support and campaign for nominees in tight races, including notable appearances by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Georgia Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, chair of the Democratic Governors Association.

On the Republican side, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Vice President JD Vance are among those who focused on the region.

Even though Republicans held on to the Florida governor seat and U.S. Senate seat, closer-than-expected margins in statewide races and House races alike make the state an attractive investment for both parties seeking to gain an edge with voters for 2028, just like Democrats' romp in historically red Texas.

Together, Texas, Florida, Georgia and North Carolina represent more than a third of the 270 electoral votes needed to win the White House.

entries.title: As budgets tighten, people are breaking out their library cards
entries.summary: Some Americans squeezed by high prices are relying more on their local libraries for things like books, streaming services and high-priced items like musical instruments and sewing machines.
entries.content:
As budgets tighten, people are breaking out their library cards

Izzy Rivera reads at least one book every week, but buying them new isn't in her budget. As she saves up for law school, some expenses don't make the cut.

"Say I'm buying a few a month," she said, "it just isn't realistic."

That's why Rivera has recently been leaning more on local libraries near her home in Topeka, Kan., checking out both physical books and digital copies on the Libby app. (Some of her recent reads: Sour Cherry by Natalia Theodoridou, Spoilt Creatures by Amy Twigg and Plastic Inc. by Beth Gardiner.) Rivera also went to her library's used book sale last month, where she picked up 15 books for about $20.

The library's money-saving potential doesn't end there for her. Rivera also watches movies on the streaming app Kanopy, reads the New York Times at no cost and often passes the time at a local branch.

"It's somewhere I can go where I'm not expected to spend money," she said. "If I were to go to a coffee shop just to get out and do something, the expectation would be to buy a coffee, even though I probably didn't want a coffee."

It is something of a truism in the library world that, when economic conditions worsen, people use libraries more. Patrons and librarians across the U.S. tell NPR they're seeing that pan out now.

Prices for food and other everyday items continue to rise in part because of the war with Iran, and affordability was a top concern among voters heading into the midterm elections. According to a Pew Research Center survey released in mid-October, 44% of Americans say they've struggled in the past year to afford at least one basic necessity, such as medical care or their rent or mortgage payment. Seventy percent of adults also said they've cut back on "extras," such as subscriptions to streaming services.

Data shared with NPR by several of the largest public library systems in the U.S. show recent upticks in cardholder membership, circulation and event attendance. Librarians say part of that can be attributed to the rising cost of living — and the growing recognition that libraries' resources extend far beyond physical books.

"People start off with Audible and then a friend tells them, 'Why are you paying for that? You can get that at the library if you're a smidgen bit patient,'" said Jeremy Reeder, director of the Maricopa County Library District in Arizona.

Of course, the rising cost of living is not the only factor driving more people to check out libraries. Many institutions have gotten better at marketing themselves, librarians say, and social media has helped foster a renewed cultural interest in reading.

"Libraries have been popular for a really long time, but I think that there's heightened awareness of the wide range of offerings that our libraries are providing," said Maria McCauley, president of the American Library Association. "They are especially popular right now, I think, because people are aware that everything that we provide is free or very low cost."

By the numbers

There is historical precedent for the idea that economic slumps are a boon to libraries.

An analysis by the American Library Association found that circulation increased at 18 large public library systems during a brief U.S. recession in 2001. Another study of 541 libraries found that library use was higher during the Great Recession than in previous years. (However, a 1986 article that tried to draw a similar correlation found no data to support that theory.)

Though it's unclear to what extent affordability concerns are pushing people to libraries now, several large public systems have reported growth in recent years.

Usage of the Los Angeles Public Library's makerspace grew 37% between the last two fiscal years, while digital circulation and library visits were both up over 20%. In-person visits, adult library card applications and Wi-Fi sessions at the Chicago Public Library all jumped by more than 11% year-over-year from January through July. The Maricopa County Library District, which has seen its cardholder base grow sharply as it moved its application process online, recorded a 34% increase in Kanopy use and a 78% surge in Hoopla use over the past three years.

The Topeka and Shawnee County Public Library, where Izzy Rivera goes, logged an 8.1% increase in digital media checkouts last year, though physical circulation is down. There's also been a surge in requests for tech support, such as help with online job applications.

OverDrive, the company that owns Kanopy, reported a 41% spike in users of the streaming service last year alone.

The landscape for libraries

In general, libraries are on a cultural come-up: They're increasingly popular among Gen Z and Millennials — even those who aren't big readers. And there's more interest in reading writ large, as social media phenomena such as #BookTok fuel book sales.

Another change in library use began during the pandemic, when lockdowns forced users to acclimate to digital media, such as the e-books and streaming apps offered by libraries. "It was already a trend pre-pandemic," said Los Angeles Public Library senior librarian Edwin Rodarte, "but the pandemic sort of boosted it and it just skyrocketed afterward."

Yet the growing popularity of libraries also comes at a time when their federal funding is under threat. Last year, the Trump administration attempted to gut the federal Institute of Museum and Library Services and cancel the grants it provides to libraries across the country. The attorneys general of 21 states sued to block the move, and the administration ultimately reinstated the grants.

But the IMLS appears to still be on the Trump administration's radar. When the White House released its budget proposal in April for the current fiscal year, it recommended zeroing out funding for the agency.

Maria McCauley, who is also director of the Cambridge Public Library in Massachusetts, said libraries rely on a combination of federal, state and local funding to operate.

"Every year, libraries have to make a case for their funding, and especially when it's uncertain, it can be harder to get all the resources that we need," she said.

"All that money we are providing back out to the community in terms of expertise, in terms of beautiful facilities for our community members" as well as collections and programs, McCauley added.

It's not just books

Librarians note that libraries are also quick to respond to public needs, and have been a community resource for locals facing issues such as homelessness or food insecurity. One survey found that 56% of libraries offered food security support services last year, the same year a Republican tax and spending bill signed by President Trump ushered in major changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, and millions of Americans started to lose food benefits.

Many libraries also offer classes, meetups and what's often called a "library of things," where they lend out items that patrons may be unable to afford or prefer not to buy: WiFi hotspots, induction cooktops, birding kits, camping gear.

At a biweekly crafting meetup called "Sew What?!" at the Free Library of Philadelphia's Parkway Central Branch, the library provides sewing machines and materials at no cost. Chloe deBeus, who was working on her Halloween costume during a recent event, said attendees can try their hand at sewing and other crafts without having to pay the potentially steep upfront costs.

"You do need to purchase yarn or you do need to purchase fabric. Maybe if you want to sew, you do need to get a machine," deBeus said. "The question is do I even enjoy it enough to purchase these things up front?"

Down the hall, Nathaniel Muns was playing a keyboard inside the branch's music department. His own keyboard had broken, and he hadn't replaced it yet. "Sometimes having a keyboard in your home is not accessible and not doable," he said.

As he practiced the jazz standard "All the Things You Are" and other songs, Muns said the cost of living had risen "astronomically." The library offered him, a recent college graduate who now works with an AI startup, a place to go.

"Being able to come to the library really helps me kind of decompress at the end of the day," he said.

entries.title: Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don't hold your breath
entries.summary: A new Democratic majority in Congress could pressure the president to end the war in Iran. But it will be harder for them to directly affect fuel prices, which are tied to a complex international oil market.
entries.content:
Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don't hold your breath

Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help

Democrats are now poised to take control of Congress by wide margins — and a critical driver of their success has been voter fury about how the war in Iran has driven up the cost of fuel.

Before the war, about one fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz. As the war throttled that waterway, the price of oil rose: A barrel of Brent crude cost about $70 in late February, spent months hovering around the $110 mark, and is now close to $95.

That's driven up the price of everything that's refined from crude. A gallon of gas costs $4.12 on average — about $1 higher than a year ago. The price of diesel hit a record high in September at $6.52, and while it's fallen a bit since then, a gallon remains about $2.50 higher than this time last year, according to AAA.

These soaring prices helped major oil companies rake in huge profits over the past two quarters, while making the cost of fuel at the pump uncomfortably high for drivers, and boosting the price of nearly everything in a nation that is heavily reliant on trucking.

So now that the midterm results are in, could drivers see lower gasoline and diesel prices anytime soon?

Not so fast, experts say. Here's why.

What could Democrats do?

Nothing yet — members of the new Congress won't be sworn in until January.

And once they are seated, U.S. legislators have limited powers to directly affect the price of oil, which is dictated by a complex global market.

In the run-up to the election, most of the actions taken by the federal government to lower fuel prices came through the White House, not Congress. Hoping to stave off losses for his party, President Trump tried to ease the cost of diesel by loosening federal rules on dyed diesel, which is normally used for farming. He also announced a deal that would bring more Russian diesel to global markets, including the U.S., by temporarily lifting sanctions. Neither of these did much to move the needle.

But the new Congressional Democrats will have the power to push the president to end the war in Iran, in part by making it harder to authorize new war spending. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D.-NY) told reporters on Wednesday that Democrats are intent on ending the war and bringing down the cost of living, saying that "relief is on the way."

"What a unified Democratic Congress can do is make escalation considerably more costly: both chambers can pass resolutions, attach conditions to war spending and hold back confirmations of key officials," Claudio Galimberti, chief economist of Rystad Energy, wrote in a market note to the media.

Still, the president has veto power over legislation, as well as executive powers. " President Trump still retains full discretionary authority over military strikes, over blockades and sanctions, licenses, and so on," said Jorge León, head of geopolitical analysis at Rystad Energy, in an interview with NPR.

Trump has sent mixed messages about whether he wants to end or escalate the war. In the past few weeks, he warned Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a new military campaign after the midterms. The U.S. struck Qeshm, an island in the Strait of Hormuz that Iran uses to launch its own strikes, on Nov. 2.

But on election night, Trump told The New York Times that he knew voters were unhappy about gas prices. And the next day, as the extent of the election rout became clear, Vice President JD Vance posted on social media: "The reason we lost is the war."

If the war ends, when would prices fall?

Jaime Brito, executive director of refining and oil markets for Dow Jones Energy, says if there's a deal to end the war, traders could be very excited. Brito said they might look for formal announcements from both Iran and the U.S. that the strait is reopening, and that both sides are pulling back their military presence in the area.

If market traders are convinced the peace will last? "If that scenario happens, then I personally see crude prices dropping, you know, $15, $20 [a barrel] immediately, in the next two, three days from the announcement," he said.

But for gasoline and diesel prices to fall, too, oil would have to start moving again. Ships that have been running long, alternative routes to avoid passing through the Strait of Hormuz would have to return to their points of origin, and then resume their former routes through the strait. León pointed out, that could lead to traffic jams.

From there, that crude will still need to be refined and make its way onto the market.

In the most optimistic scenario, Brito said, it could take three months after a ceasefire or deal is announced for gasoline and diesel prices to hit their prewar levels.

León thinks it would take more like six months for the price of crude to hit its prewar level, and then another month or two for gasoline and diesel to follow. But that's assuming all goes well. And, both of them said, there could be hiccups along the way that stretch the recovery timeline out for up to a year after a deal is announced.

" I don't want to say this, but, you know, expensive gasoline prices could be a new normal," Brito said.

The X factors

The first big X factor: the war in Ukraine.

If Ukraine continues attacking Russian refineries, the price of diesel may not drop as precipitously as gasoline might. That's because Russia's refineries normally bring much of the world's diesel to global markets. Resuming traffic through the Strait of Hormuz will help lower the price of diesel — but it may take longer to reach its prewar level, León said.

Other scenarios could make for a less rosy picture, León said. U.S. refineries have been running above 90% capacity — what if they need emergency maintenance just at the moment when there's more oil ready to bring to market? Or, what if hostilities restart again, despite a deal?

Brito agreed. Before the end of the year, there could theoretically be new attacks in the strait, he wrote, "if the current administration sees it as a 'window' to complete unfinished tasks before the new Congressional layout takes their seat in January."

And there's also one more factor at play: The war has raised the price of moving oil itself around the world.

Since the Strait of Hormuz has been blocked off for so long, freight costs have gone up; ships carrying oil have had to skirt around the strait, take longer routes and use more fuel in the process. Plus, the price of insuring those ships has gone up, since transit around the strait has gotten so much riskier.

That means that even the oil industry is paying more to be in the oil business. And if hostilities persist and those freight costs remain high, that could keep the price of Brent crude elevated for longer.

"Bottom line," Brito wrote, for any hope of a return to normal prices, "you need to see a definitive end of the conflict."

entries.title: Bob Dylan comes knockin' on pope's door as Leo welcomes legend to Vatican
entries.summary: The American singer-songwriter and poet visited with the American pope at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy. The Vatican said the encounter was brief.
entries.content:
Bob Dylan comes knockin' on pope's door as Leo welcomes legend to Vatican

VATICAN CITY — Bob Dylan came knockin' on Pope Leo XIV' s door Wednesday, as the American singer-songwriter and poet visited with the American pope at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy.

The Vatican said the encounter was brief, with Leo giving Dylan a rosary and Dylan presenting the pope with a copy of his autobiography, "Chronicles: Volume One."

Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan penned in 1963, "Go Away You Bomb," in his 2026 book "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift."

Leo was warning against the race to rearm and the recourse to nuclear weapons and quoted the lyric, addressed to a hypothetical atomic bomb: "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled."

Two Vatican officials accompanied Dylan: the Rev. Antonio Spadaro, a Vatican culture ministry official who also accompanied Patti Smith to a July audience with Leo; and Andrea Monda, the editor of the Vatican newspaper, L'Osservatore Romano.

Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with Leo, and the two met in private for a few minutes. In an essay in L'Osservatore Romano, he recalled that the former Robert Prevost, who was born in Chicago in 1955, grew up familiar with Dylan's music.

He also noted that Dylan was very familiar with St. Augustine of Hippo, the inspiration of Leo's spirituality and Augustinian religious order, penning "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine" for the 1967 album John Wesley Harding.

Dylan, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2016, wore a black hoodie and a loose tie. Vatican photos of the encounter showed him with the hood over his head.

It wasn't Dylan's first papal encounter: He played for Pope John Paul II, and thousands of other people, in 1997 during a concert capping a religious congress in Bologna, Italy.

Dylan, who changed his name from Robert Zimmerman, was born to a Jewish family in Minnesota. He famously became a born-again Christian in 1979 and alienated some of his longtime fans with songs like "Gotta Serve Somebody" and "Saved."

In more recent years, Dylan has been more circumspect about his religious beliefs. In a 2022 interview with the Wall Street Journal, Dylan said that he was a "religious person" who reads the scriptures, meditates and prays.

Dylan met with Leo in between concert dates in Italy. He played in Milan on Monday and is playing Rome on Thursday. In his most recent concert before the meeting with the pope, Dylan sang his 1997 song "Tryin' to Get to Heaven" that contains the lyric, "I've been all around the world, boys/Now I'm trying to get to heaven before they close the door."

entries.title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison
entries.summary: Wong was sentenced for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement.
entries.content:
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison

HONG KONG — Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement.

Wong was charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under the law. In September, he pleaded guilty to the offense, a move that can typically reduce the sentence.

The 30-year-old is already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term for the city's biggest national security case linked to an unofficial primary after entering a guilty plea in that case. Before being prosecuted for the collusion-related charge, Wong had been expected to be freed in January 2027.

Judge William Tam said during the sentencing hearing that Wong's offense was of a grave nature and rejected that his role was limited.

He also said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong's guilty plea.

Wong looked calm and thanked his supporters before leaving the court. His supporters waved to him and Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism, once led by Wong, was in tears.

The judge said Wong could serve his two prison sentences concurrently. Wong only has about two months left on the sentence for his previous national security conviction.

Resident ET Wong said that when Joshua Wong was just teenager, he possessed "big-picture thinking" that some adults might not even have. He walked a difficult path for Hong Kong's future, human rights and student movement, she said.

"At least in my heart, he should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment," she said.

Wong's convictions seen as discouraging dissent

Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society marked by its vibrant protest and media scenes. But after an anti-government movement rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for their reports critical of the government shut down, and dozens of civil society groups dissolved.

Observers say Wong's sentencing shows the authorities' determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible, further chilling civic activism.

"NSL charges can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary," said Eric Lai, a research fellow at Georgetown Center for Asian Law, referring to the national security law.

But Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities also said the security law is crucial for the city's stability following the 2019 protests, maintaining that the city's law enforcement actions were evidence-based.

Prosecution highlights Wong's lobbying and advocacy efforts

The prosecution previously alleged that Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination. It said that before the security law was introduced, the pair had been calling for sanctions and other adverse measures against Hong Kong and China. It pointed to his meetings with U.S. politicians like Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio in 2016 and 2019.

After the law was enacted, Law and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw foreign countries' attention and bolster the request for sanctions, blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said.

His lawyer Derek Chan earlier urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release.

His friends said during his nearly six years in prison, Wong kept reading books and exercising, teaching himself guitar while maturing in his thinking.

To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong's British colonial rule before the city's return to China in 1997.

Despite being held behind bars, Wong's influence appears to have remained a concern, at least for the pro-Beijing camp.

In September, a pro-Beijing newspaper report criticized a 2017 documentary about Wong on Netflix for "beautifying" his crimes. The city's security bureau told local media the government was taking follow-up action.

But the documentary then shot to the top of Netflix's popular chart in Hong Kong.

entries.title: Where voters stand on state ballot measures, from abortion to LGBTQ rights to guns
entries.summary: Voters in dozens of states considered 146 statewide ballot measures this midterm cycle, on topics spanning LGBTQ rights, wealth taxes, abortion, redistricting, guns and more.
entries.content:
Where voters stand on state ballot measures, from abortion to LGBTQ rights to guns

Tuesday's midterm elections were a huge sweep for Democrats, among other takeaways.

And across 39 states — plus Washington, D.C. and the Northern Mariana Islands — voters weighed in on 146 statewide ballot measures spanning issues from taxes to transgender rights to traffic cameras to data centers and AI.

Here's a look at some of those results.

Three states moved to preserve abortion access

The U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, leaving the legality and regulation of abortion up to each state. In subsequent elections, over a dozen states have put access to abortion on their ballots — and overwhelmingly moved to secure it.

This year, four states considered abortion measures. Three passed, while Idaho voted to preserve the state's abortion ban from 2022.

In Missouri, voters rejected a Republican-led amendment that would have banned abortion with few exceptions. The move affirms support for abortion just two years after voters mobilized to reject Missouri's ban, which was one of the strictest in the country.

Loading...

Nevada residents voted to enshrine abortion up to the point of viability in their constitution. They did so for the second election in a row, since state law requires a proposed constitutional amendment to pass twice.

Virginians voted to create a "fundamental right to reproductive freedom" in their constitution. That includes the right to an abortion during the first two trimesters (and afterward in certain cases), as well as the right to contraception, fertility, postpartum care and more.

States voted on voting

Many states considered changes to how they run their elections.

It was too early to call Wednesday afternoon whether voters had approved some of the more far-reaching changes, in Alaska and Arizona.

Other states — including Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio — passed measures toughening identification requirements for voters, while California voted against such an effort.

Several states — including Alaska, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia — approved measures reinforcing that U.S. citizenship is required to vote in their elections.

Redistricting was also top of mind for voters. President Trump kicked off a redistricting race earlier this year by urging Republican-led states to redraw their districts ahead of the midterms. Republicans and Democrats in multiple states did so. But many of the districts altered to boost GOP prospects ultimately went to Democratic candidates.

Missouri voters rejected a Republican-friendly congressional map, while Maryland voters passed a redistricting amendment that could pave the way for a Democrat-leaning map in 2028.

Loading...

Virginians passed a measure automatically restoring voting rights to anyone convicted of a felony once they have completed their sentence.

A mixed bag for LGBTQ rights

Virginians also passed a constitutional amendment officially repealing its ban on gay marriage and adding language confirming that the commonwealth will recognize marriage between two adults regardless of their sex, gender or race.

Virginia's ban has been moot since the Supreme Court made same-sex marriage legal nationwide in 2015, but this measure is seen as a safeguard in case Obergefell v. Hodges gets reversed (as some have feared in the wake of the court's overturning of Roe v. Wade). Other states have made similar moves, including Colorado and California in 2024.

Vermont overwhelmingly voted to add an amendment to its constitution guaranteeing equal protection under the law "race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin."

A number of states considered measures restricting transgender kids' access to school sports teams and gender-affirming care, with Colorado passing both. A Washington state measure to ban trans students from competing in girls' school sports was still leading on Wednesday.

Arizona passed a proposal requiring schools and athletic associations to restrict students, athletes and employees from using facilities — including restrooms, locker rooms, and other private spaces — that are not designated for their sex assigned at birth. Arizona law already bans trans girls from playing on school sports teams designated for girls, and this measure would extend that prohibition to recreational organizations like Little League.

Loading...

Taxes and state spending up for debate

One of the most high-profile ballot measures asked Floridians to weigh cutting property taxes for homeowners, which critics say would take billions of dollars in local government revenue away from much-needed public services like food banks, libraries, transportation and infrastructure. Voters overwhelmingly passed the amendment.

In California, voters pondered whether to approve a one-off 5% tax on individuals with more than $1 billion in assets, with most of the money raised going toward health care services. The fight against that ballot measure was one of the most expensive in the state's history. The contest is too close to call as of Wednesday afternoon.

Loading...

Tennessee voters approved a constitutional amendment prohibiting its government from levying a statewide property tax, which it has not collected since 1949. Arizona voters passed a measure that bans cities and towns from raising taxes on groceries until July 2027. North Carolinians approved an amendment to cap the maximum personal income tax at 3.5%.

Washington voters considered whether to repeal an income tax on individuals and households earning more than $1 million, which is scheduled to take effect in 2028. Early results indicate they want to keep that tax.

A polar-opposite pair of gun ballot measures

Massachusetts voted to keep a 2024 law tightening firearm regulations. The law made Massachusetts gun control measures among the strictest in the nation, as it also included requiring "ghost guns" to have a serial number, broadened the definition of "assault-style firearm" and expanded the state's red flag laws.

Meanwhile, in Idaho, a ballot measure asked voters for help choosing the official state gun from six different brands and models. The Winchester Model 1873 — aka the "Gun that Won the West" — leads in the polls as of Wednesday, though the state legislature would need to pass a separate law to make the winner official.

The ballot initiatives about data centers

At least 38 jurisdictions voted on the sprawling facilities needed to power AI, and Tuesday revealed how many voters dislike them. Jurisdictions in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, and Wisconsin voted to restrict data centers.

Of these, at least 12 localities voted to restrict the size of data centers, while six others voted to halt development and ban construction of all facilities, according to Data Centers on the Ballot.

The one community that supported data centers is in Harwood, North Dakota, where 75% of voters did not want to place restrictions on industrial projects, including data centers.

Ohio, one of the frontline states on the issue, had 21 ballot measures mentioning data centers. Voters there moved to restrict the AI facilities: Trenton, Ohio voted to ban data centers over 25 megawatts, while Hubbard moved to ban construction of data centers of any size, including converting existing buildings. Ohio voters also rejected rezoning areas from rural residential to light industrial for data center usage.

Candidates spent up to $40 million on ads about data centers this election cycle. They were a contentious issue in many statewide elections, as 77% of Americans say they are concerned about data centers raising electricity costs, according to a June Reuters/Ipsos poll. The poll also showed two-thirds of Democrats and half of Republicans said they'd oppose a data center in their community.

Other honorable mentions

Alabama voters passed ballot measures requiring local school boards to adopt policies directing public K-12 schools to recite the Pledge of Allegiance and, separately, play or perform the first stanza of "The Star-Spangled Banner" at least once a week during school hours.

In Arizona, voters passed a measure banning the state from installing and using photo enforcement systems (like speed and red-light cameras) to catch people who violate certain traffic ordinances.

Residents of Washington, D.C. had just one ballot initiative to consider: banning the controversial duck or goose liver dish known as foie gras. The debate went viral in recent days, prompting a slew of Halloween costumes, a four-course restaurant tasting menu and public appearances by a real duck named Olivia. D.C. voted overwhelmingly to prohibit the force-feeding of birds to enlarge their livers, and the sale of the delicacy itself. Across the country, voters in Denver approved a similar measure.

entries.title: Elon Musk will face scrutiny from Democrats after midterms
entries.summary: Democrats are likely to launch investigations into Musk's influence, including his leadership of DOGE and government contracts
entries.content:
Elon Musk will face scrutiny from Democrats after midterms

Elon Musk wasn't on Tuesday's ballot, but he stands to lose a lot from Democrats' sweeping midterm victories in the House and Senate. In no state was this more acutely felt than in Texas, home to the headquarters of Musk's companies and where he spent more than $200 million, according to federal filings, in a mission to sway the Senate race in the Republican candidate's favor.

With a Democratic majority in Congress, the billionaire, who controls Tesla and SpaceX, will likely face investigations into the billions of dollars of government contracts his companies have been awarded since President Trump returned to office and his role leading the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of Trump's second term.

Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings analyzed by OpenSecrets, a nonprofit that tracks campaign spending. That makes him the top donor in the midterms and among the very largest political donors in American history.

The central question Democratic lawmakers say they want answered is whether Musk used his influence inside the Trump administration to benefit his own businesses, and whether taxpayer money, government data and public institutions were put at risk in the process.

During the four months Musk led DOGE, he received at least $6.3 billion in government contracts. Since then, he has gained at least another $10 billion in government contracts, according to the Democracy Defenders Fund, a legal advocacy nonprofit.

"The DOGE chickens are coming home to roost. Elon Musk waved a chainsaw on stage and laughed while firing public servants and gutting the services Americans rely on. Then he lied to the American people about the savings. He must answer for it under oath," Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) wrote on X.

Musk's foreign dealings are also under scrutiny. Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware posted on X that Musk's links to Russia's President Vladimir Putin are "One more thing to add to the list of questions for Musk when I subpoena him."

U.S. Rep. Mike Levin of California highlighted that Musk restricted Ukraine's use of his Starlink satellite internet service days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia and began buying Russian diesel in October. Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, are vital for Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, frontline communications and drone operations in its war against Russia.

"How on earth did we get to this point? How is it possible that Musk can disrupt an American ally's military operations whenever he chooses, maintain a clear line to the Kremlin, and face zero accountability to the American people or the U.S. government?" Levin wrote on X.

Musk did not respond to a request for comment from NPR.

While leading DOGE, Musk was a part-time special government employee, and as such was subject to a federal law prohibiting covered executive branch and related personnel from participating in official matters affecting their personal financial interests, said Richard Painter, former chief White House ethics lawyer in the George W. Bush administration.

"SpaceX is a big contractor and gets a lot of money from NASA and the Department of Defense. If [Musk] touched anything that he knew would have an impact on SpaceX, he would've committed a crime," Painter said.

Texas has played a growing role in Musk's business empire

Texas in particular has become a big focus of Musk's efforts to exert political power, as he has made the state the nerve center of his sprawling business empire. Tesla's corporate headquarters and a major vehicle manufacturing facility are in Austin. X, formerly Twitter, is based outside of Austin. SpaceX, which makes rockets and satellites, is based in southern Texas. Musk's Neuralink and The Boring Company are also headquartered in the state.

Much of Musk's estimated wealth is tied up in his ownership stakes in his companies. Even as markets rose Wednesday after Democrats' midterm wins, SpaceX shares fell nearly 4% and Tesla dropped 3%.

SpaceX is reportedly exploring several possible Texas sites for large data centers. Tesla owns and operates its massive Giga Texas data center in Austin. In August, plans for a $16.8 billion SpaceXAI semiconductor fabrication project in Texas were announced.

Musk directed at least $225 million of his midterm spending to Texas, according to OpenSecrets, including supporting Republican Ken Paxton's bid for U.S. Senate and Gov. Greg Abbott's reelection campaign.

But Paxton and Abbott both lost, suggesting Musk's money wasn't enough to overcome a wave of enthusiasm that saw Democrats capture every statewide office in Texas.

"Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas," said James Talarico, who defeated Paxton in the Senate race, at a campaign rally in Lubbock last month.

Elon Musk's own posts on X about Talarico were often personal and incendiary. "Talarico will vote to trans your kids," he wrote on Nov. 1.

Talarico addressed Musk in his victory speech on Tuesday.

"We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country. Power belongs to the people," Talarico said. "The real fight in this country is not right versus left; it is top versus bottom."

As results came in on Tuesday night, Musk wrote on X, "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," followed by a shrug emoji.
